title: A Tiny Red Plant With a Death Hug
summary:
Beside lakes in Florida lives a small plant that eats insects, with bright red thread-like leaves. In August 2026 it was named its own species, Drosera floridana.

Plant expert Lilly Anderson-Messec first saw it in 2014 and thought it looked special, though it was first called a type of a common sundew whose closest group lived hundreds of miles away.

Noah Juve, a student at the University of Florida, wrote the paper that made it its own species. He and Andreas Fleischmann compared it with close cousins at over 100 places. It stood out for its color, seeds, flowers and bloom time.

The plant hunts in a strange way. Sticky drops work like flypaper. They trap small insects. Then it wraps around them and breaks them down. People call this the slow-motion death hug.

Its home is very small. It grows only on sandy lake edges in an area about 12 miles by 16 miles. It lives in only two counties in Florida, Washington and Bay.

Naming it matters. Such plants can stay hidden from protection work. As Juve said, "If something doesn't have a name, how can you conserve it?"
why_it_matters: Naming a new plant helps people protect it before its tiny home disappears.
